\chapter{Synthesis --- the Same Sentence, Two Continents}
\label{ch:spanish-synthesis-plural-you}
\hlchaptermodality{33}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can choose between vosotros and ustedes by where I am, and say that neither corrects the other.}

The first choice in this book decided by geography rather than meaning.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — the same sentence, two continents}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-sintesis-dos-continentes}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new here. Say \emph{hablan}, then \emph{habláis}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a choice that is not about grammar}]
Every other choice this book has asked you to make has been about \textbf{meaning}. \emph{Tú} or \emph{usted} — how close are you to this person? \emph{El} or \emph{un} — does your listener already know which one you mean?

This one is different. It is about \textbf{where you are}.

\begin{quote}
— ¿\textbf{Habláis} español? — \emph{asked in Madrid, to friends.} — ¿\textbf{Hablan} ustedes español? — \emph{asked in Bogotá, to the same friends.}
\end{quote}

Identical meaning. Identical register. The speaker chose by geography, and nothing else.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
This matters more than a regional footnote, because it settles what \textquotedblleft{}correct Spanish\textquotedblright{} means in this book.

\textbf{Neither of those sentences is the correction of the other.} Roughly 40 million people use \emph{vosotros} daily; several hundred million have never used it in their lives and never will. A course that taught only \emph{ustedes} would leave you unable to follow a Spanish film. One that taught only \emph{vosotros} would leave you sounding strange in nineteen countries.

So you learn both, and you learn \emph{which is which} — which is exactly what you have just done across four chapters.

\begin{quote}
If you must pick one to produce: \textbf{ustedes}. It is understood everywhere, Spain included, and in the Americas it is the only option.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the Madrid version, then the Bogotá version
  \item the one you would actually use, and say why
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What decides between \emph{habláis} and \emph{hablan}? (\textbf{Where you are} — not what you mean.) Which is correct? (\textbf{Both.}) And which one will carry you everywhere? (\textbf{Ustedes hablan}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
